title: Forty Shillings a Day: The Solar Kit M-KOPA Sold Through M-Pesa
dek: In 2012 M-KOPA's founders chose to sell solar kits on credit, paid for in daily M-Pesa instalments below a family's kerosene bill.

story.founder: Jesse Moore, Nick Hughes, Chad Larson
story.event: Launching pay-as-you-go solar kits paid for in daily M-Pesa instalments
story.summary: M-KOPA, founded by Jesse Moore, Nick Hughes and Chad Larson, began commercial sales in Kenya in June 2012 and in October 2012 launched with Safaricom a d.light solar kit sold for a 2,500-shilling deposit and 40 shillings a day through M-Pesa, with a SIM in each unit that cut the light if payments stopped. After pilots in which it dropped renting and hourly charging, it had over 1,000 customers that October, about 50,000 by February 2014 and more than 300,000 households by early 2016.
paragraphs: In late October 2012, Safaricom and a young company called M-KOPA put a solar kit on sale through 75 shops in the farming towns of Eldoret and Kitale. At the Eldoret launch, M-KOPA's managing director, Jesse Moore, stood beside Safaricom's chief executive, Bob Collymore. The d.light kit had a small rooftop panel, a control box, three lamps and phone chargers. It cost 16,900 shillings, but nobody had to find that sum at once: a 2,500-shilling deposit, then 40 shillings a day through M-Pesa for a year, after which the kit was theirs.

The offer rested on what the founders knew. Nick Hughes had helped start M-Pesa at Vodafone in 2004; Moore, a Canadian, had also worked at Vodafone, and later said M-KOPA's "germination goes back to those early days of M-Pesa." Their co-founder Chad Larson became chief credit officer. Off-grid families were spending about 50 shillings a day on kerosene and phone charging, Bloomberg reported, and a grid connection cost at least 35,000 shillings. Moore pitched the kit as "a modern, cleaner and longer-lasting technology for less than what they would spend on kerosene."

Success was not assured. In 2011, while M-KOPA was raising money, the Gates Foundation declined to invest. Those who did invest included Gray Ghost Ventures, the Shell Foundation and Britain's Department for International Development. A pilot in the Rift Valley went well, and commercial sales began in June 2012. The pilots also corrected the founders. Hughes later said they had considered renting kits out rather than selling them, and at first charged for hours of use: "Of course we switched after experimenting." They settled on a sale on credit, with a SIM card in each unit that cut the light if payments stopped.

At the October launch Moore said, "We have over 1,000 customers in Kenya already," and the company hoped for tens of thousands within a year. By February 2014 it had about 50,000 customers and had borrowed 1.72 billion shillings from the Commercial Bank of Africa and the Gates Foundation. By early 2016 more than 300,000 households in East Africa had been connected. Hughes later said a scalable model was "all about trust from that customer, especially when it comes to low-income people."

quote.text: Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with your brother smile—and get a witness; for trust and mistrust, alike ruin men.
quote.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg eBook #348
quote.connection: Hughes said M-KOPA's model was all about customers' trust, yet every kit carried a SIM that could switch the light off. Hesiod, advising his brother, would not call that a contradiction: smile, fix the terms, get a witness. His warning is that trust alone and mistrust alone each do damage.

reflection: M-KOPA handed families a kit worth months of income on the strength of a 2,500-shilling deposit, and in the same box placed a way to switch it off. Neither half would have worked without the other, and both were stated plainly at the start.

Somewhere this week you will be relying on someone's word: a colleague who says a task is done, a supplier's delivery date, a relative's promise. Trust with no check at all can sour a working relationship as surely as suspicion does. A check agreed in advance, the same for everyone, is different from one sprung out of doubt. It lets people be trusted without anyone having to pretend.
invitation: Think of one arrangement at work or at home that rests on someone's word alone. Today, suggest one simple, agreed way for both of you to see how it is going, and offer it as help rather than suspicion.

cross_checks.claim: The 2012 kit cost 16,900 shillings, paid as a 2,500-shilling deposit and 40 shillings a day through M-Pesa.
M-KOPA had about 1,000 customers by October 2012.
Nick Hughes had helped start M-Pesa at Vodafone.
Each unit could be switched off remotely if payments stopped.
The Commercial Bank of Africa and the Gates Foundation lent to M-KOPA (Sh1.72 billion by February 2014).
More than 300,000 households had been connected by early 2016.

research_notes: Launch date: Bloomberg (October 2012) and London Business School (2013) say commercial sales began in June 2012 with Safaricom; ITWeb (24 October 2012) reports the Safaricom rollout through 75 shops in Eldoret and Kitale that month; CNBC (2015) says 'late 2012'; Business Daily (February 2014) says operations began '15 months ago' and captions a 2012 Eldoret launch; MIT Technology Review (2016, not cited) says 2011, which matches LBS's founding year rather than sales. The story says sales began in June and opens on the October rollout. Founding year: LBS says established in 2011; How we made it in Africa says Hughes co-founded M-KOPA in 2012; Wikipedia (not cited) says a 2010 start-up became M-KOPA in 2011; the story avoids a founding year. Prices changed over time: 2,500 deposit, 40 shillings a day and 16,900 total in 2012 (Bloomberg, ITWeb); 2,999 upfront, 50 a day and about 20,999 in 2014 (Business Daily); about $35 deposit and 45-50 US cents a day in 2015-16 (CNBC, TechCrunch); SSIR gives about $29 down. The story uses only the 2012 figures. Customer numbers rise consistently: over 1,000 (October 2012), about 50,000 (February 2014), over 150,000 (CNBC, February 2015), more than 300,000 (SSIR, January 2016; TechCrunch, April 2016), 425,000 (How we made it in Africa, October 2016); the story stops at 300,000. Kit specification: Bloomberg 2012 says a 4-watt panel; later models were 8 watts (CNBC 2015); the story says 'a small rooftop panel'. Funding is set to 'mixed' rather than the slate's 'venture': the first backers combined an impact venture fund (Gray Ghost Ventures) with grants from the Shell Foundation and DFID (Bloomberg; SSIR says grant funding reached $10 million) and later loans from CBA and the Gates Foundation. Chad Larson's role is from SSIR (2016), which calls him co-founder and chief credit officer; the story says he 'became' chief credit officer without dating it. Hughes's remarks on renting and hourly charging come from a 2016 interview and are attributed as later recollection. Safaricom's own October 2012 press release and the GSMA interview with Hughes block the checker and are not cited; Bloomberg's 2015 feature could not be read and is not cited. The Hesiod lines are advice to his brother Perses on household dealings and are applied by analogy.
